questions.text: Which of the following is true for the language $\{a^p\mid p\text{ is a prime}\}$?
questions.optA: It is not accepted by a Turing Machine
questions.optB: It is regular but not context-free
questions.optC: It is context-free but not regular
questions.optD: It is neither regular nor context-free, but accepted by a Turing machine
questions.referenceAnswer: Primality is decidable, so a Turing machine can accept exactly the unary prime lengths. Every unary context-free language is regular. The prime lengths are not eventually periodic (and hence not a unary regular language): pumping a sufficiently large prime-length accepted word would produce a composite length. Thus it is neither regular nor context-free, but decidable.

questions.text: Which of the following are decidable? I. Whether the intersection of two regular languages is infinite II. Whether a given context-free language is regular III. Whether two push-down automata accept the same language IV. Whether a given grammar is context-free
questions.subject: 2. TOC
questions.referenceAnswer: I is decidable: construct the product DFA and check for a reachable cycle that can reach a final state. II (regularity of a general CFL) and III (equivalence of arbitrary PDAs) are undecidable. IV is decidable by checking whether each production has exactly one nonterminal on its left, the syntactic CFG condition. Thus I and IV.

If the secondary index is built on the key field of the file, and a multilevel index scheme is used to store the secondary index, the number of first-level and second-level blocks in the multilevel index are respectively
questions.subject: 12. DBMS
questions.referenceAnswer: A dense secondary index has one entry per record, of $6+10=16$ bytes. A 1024-byte block holds 64 entries. Thus the first level needs $16384/64=256$ blocks; the next level needs $256/64=4$. Data-file ordering on a non-key field does not make this key index sparse.

The subset-sum problem is defined as follows. Given a set of $n$ positive integers, $S=\{a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots,a_n\}$, and a positive integer $W$, is there a subset of $S$ whose elements sum to $W$? A dynamic program for solving this problem uses a 2-dimensional Boolean array, $X$, with $n$ rows and $W+1$ columns. $X[i,j]$, $1\le i\le n$, $0\le j\le W$, is TRUE if and only if there is a subset of $\{a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_i\}$ whose elements sum to $j$.
Which of the following is valid for $2\le i\le n$ and $a_i\le j\le W$?
questions.subject: 7. Algorithms
questions.referenceAnswer: A subset summing to j either excludes a_i, giving X[i-1,j], or includes it once, requiring a subset of the previous i-1 values summing to j-a_i. Use OR to combine these cases. Referring to row i in the second term could reuse a_i; AND would wrongly demand both cases.
